title: Attention is limited
hook: we can truly attend to only a little at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the invisible gorilla: viewers so busy counting passes that a gorilla walked by unseen. Your line was what am I missing. Did asking it show you anything? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

A kitchen at six in the evening. A pot is about to boil over. A child is telling a long story about recess. A phone buzzes on the counter, and the radio is reading the news. All four are asking for the same thing at once, and somehow it seems possible to give it to all of them. Then the pot boils over, and the child says, you're not listening. Both are right. Yesterday's gorilla showed what a focused beam leaves in the dark. Today asks a plainer question: how wide can the beam be?
screen: `A POT, A CHILD, A PHONE, THE NEWS.` → `YOU'RE NOT LISTENING.` → `HOW WIDE IS THE BEAM?`

segments.voice: William James answered in The Principles of Psychology. Attention, he wrote, is "the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought." One, out of several. And notice the small word seem. Several things seem possible at once. The kitchen seems manageable. But the clear, vivid kind of attention takes one at a time. Then James names the price: attention "implies withdrawal from some things in order to deal effectively with others." Every yes is also a quiet no. To truly hear the child, something has to drop away, even for a moment. Some psychologists since James describe attention as a limited capacity. On that view, simple, practiced things can go together, like walking and talking, but for anything that needs real thought, the mind moves between tasks rather than holding them all. Here's why that matters on a Tuesday. If attention is limited, it's not endless background noise. It's something precious, closer to a gift than a utility. Where it goes is what a person is actually spending. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh wrote about washing the dishes only to wash the dishes, not to hurry through them toward the next thing. That isn't a rule against busy kitchens. It's an honest admission of the same limit James described: a little at a time is how a mind really works.
screen: `ONE OUT OF WHAT SEEM SEVERAL.` · `EVERY YES IS A QUIET NO.` · `A LIMITED CAPACITY.` · `WASH THE DISHES TO WASH THE DISHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one thing to attend to. Settle, and choose it now. It could be the breath, one sound in the room, or an object in your hand, a cup, a stone, a pen. For these two minutes, give it the clear, vivid kind of attention James described. Its weight. Its edges. Its temperature. When the other things in your life knock, and they will, let them wait outside the door, and come back to the one. The bell holds the time.
Attention is limited. The mind holds one thing clearly at a time, and every yes to something is a quiet no to something else. Today's word.
Your line: a little at a time. Today, when someone talks to you, set down whatever's in your hand and give them the one clear beam. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Some contemplative teachers train single-pointed attention by asking students to do one ordinary task, like washing dishes or walking, with full attention; psychologists study the same limit by measuring how performance drops when people split attention.

fork.setup: the pot is boiling, the phone is buzzing, and your child is telling you about recess. by James's account, what can you give clear, vivid attention to?
options: all three at once, if you try hard.
one, while the others drop away for a moment.
none of them; the mind just blurs.
fork.reveal: one out of what seem several. to deal effectively with one, the mind withdraws from the others.

trapdoor: what you thought: attention is limited means I'm bad at multitasking.
what it means: every mind takes clear things one at a time. every yes to one thing is a quiet no to others.

what a scholar hears: James's definition in The Principles of Psychology, where the key word is seem: several objects seem simultaneously possible, and attention implies withdrawal from some to deal with others.
